title: Comment on "Observation of Kardar--Parisi--Zhang universal scaling in two dimensions"
authors: J. Bloch, M. Escalera, Q. Fontaine, F. Helluin, A. Minguzzi, L. Canet, S. Ravets
abstract: In their paper published in Science 392, 221 (2026), Widmann and collaborators reported interferometry experiments to explore the emission coherence decay of a two-dimensional polariton condensate generated in an array of coupled resonators. The authors claim evidence of Kardar--Parisi--Zhang (KPZ) universal scaling in the measured spatio-temporal coherence decay. We argue in the following that the data were not properly analyzed. We re-analyze the experimental data acquired both with the square and the triangular lattices for various values of the excitation power. Instead of stretched exponential decays, in the space (time) windows considered in the paper we find that the measured $|g^{(1)}(δ{\bf r}, δt)|$ at $δt=0$ ($|δ{\bf r}| $ close to $0$) rather show Gaussian (exponential) decay for all excitation powers. As a result, using as temporal and spatial exponents $β=0.5$ and $χ=1$, the data for all pump powers are found to collapse onto a single curve, which is not the KPZ scaling function. In particular, we show that the data collapse onto the KPZ scaling function presented in the paper is an artifact stemming from incorrect data normalization. We thus conclude that the main claim of the paper is not justified as the spatio-temporal decays of the coherence over the space-time windows analyzed in the paper are not well described by the KPZ universal behavior.
summary: The paper critically re-examines claims of KPZ universal scaling observed in the coherence decay of a 2D polariton condensate. By re-analyzing the interferometry data, the authors argue that the apparent KPZ collapse is due to improper data normalization. They conclude that the decay is more accurately modeled by a simple exponential time decay and Gaussian spatial decay.
main_problem: The paper challenges a claim of Kardar–Parisi–Zhang (KPZ) universal scaling observed in the spatio-temporal coherence decay of a 2D polariton condensate.
main_result: Re-analysis shows that the data collapse is better described by an exponential decay in time and Gaussian decay in space, suggesting the original KPZ claim was an artifact of incorrect data normalization.
method: The authors re-analyzed interferometry experimental data on both square and triangular lattices, comparing fits to KPZ scaling theory against a simple exponential-Gaussian model using data collapse techniques.
model_or_system: The physical system is a two-dimensional polariton condensate generated in an array of coupled resonators. The analysis focuses on the decay of the first-order correlation function, g(1)(delta r, delta t).
key_observables: First-order coherence function, |g(1)|, measured as a function of spatial separation (delta r) and time delay (delta t).
important_parameters: Excitation power, lattice geometry (square/triangular), and the exponents used in scaling laws (e.g., beta=0.5, chi=1 vs. KPZ values).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that proper normalization ($\kappa$) is crucial for correctly identifying the underlying physical decay mechanism.
figures_summary: Figures compare data fits on square and triangular lattices, showing systematic agreement with exponential-Gaussian models while demonstrating how incorrect normalization can force a misleading collapse onto KPZ scaling functions.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure of critique: first, identifying the claim in prior work; second, re-analyzing the raw data using multiple fitting frameworks (KPZ vs. Exponential-Gaussian); and finally, quantitatively demonstrating that the simpler model provides a superior fit across all tested regimes.
why_interesting: This is highly relevant as it deals with non-equilibrium dynamics and universal scaling in interacting quantum systems (polaritons), directly challenging established theoretical interpretations of experimental data in AMO/Quantum Optics.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
